system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-05-11 18:06:00 to 2177-05-14 15:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) complicated by cirrhosis was admitted with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever, concerning for recurrent cholangitis. She was started on intravenous meropenem, with improvement in symptoms and liver enzymes. An ERCP was performed, which showed no treatable strictures or stones, though a biliary biopsy was obtained. A PICC line was placed to complete a five-day course of ertapenem at home. Her diarrhea was evaluated and found to be C. difficile negative, likely due to recent antibiotics. She was discharged on a plan to transition to rifaximin after finishing IV therapy, with instructions to follow up with gastroenterology and schedule a colonoscopy. Her chronic conditions, including hypertension and hypothyroidism, were managed, and she returned to baseline function.
problems: Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Esophageal varices without mention of bleeding

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ female with primary sclerosing cholangitis now
presenting with worsening right upper quadrant pain and fever.

COMPARISON:  Right upper quadrant ultrasound from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale and Doppler ultrasound images were obtained.

FINDINGS:  The liver is echogenic and coarse in architecture, unchanged from
prior.  No definite hepatic lesion is identified.  The main portal vein is
patent with hepatopetal flow.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy. 
The patient has a known 7 mm stone within a right intrahepatic duct, findings
which are unchanged compared to prior examination.  No further upstream
dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts is noted.  The common bile duct remains
prominent, measuring 7 mm.  Debris also appears seen within the common bile
duct.  The spleen is enlarged measuring 15 cm.  No ascites is evident.  The
pancreas is not visualized due to overlying bowel gas.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Echogenic coarsened liver.  Splenomegaly.  No ascites.
2.  Again seen intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts with again seen right
hepatic duct stone.

REASON FOR EXAM:  ___ years old woman with new PICC.

COMPARISON:  Exam is compared to chest x-ray of ___.

FINDINGS:  AP portable single view chest x-ray shows new left PICC with tip
ending in lower SVC.  Right PICC has been removed.  Lung volume is normal
without nodules or consolidation.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal.

IMPRESSION:  New left PICC without complication.  No acute cardiopulmonary
processes.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having right upper quadrant pain and fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had this before—usually means my cholangitis is flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on ciprofloxacin recently, correct? And finished it just before this started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I finished the last dose the morning before I started feeling worse. I had chills, nausea, and the pain came back—same as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve had joint aches too, in your wrists and ankles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that always happens when I get these flares. It’s like my body knows something’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your ultrasound from tonight. It shows your liver still has that coarse texture, and your spleen is enlarged, which we expected. But importantly, the 7mm stone in your right intrahepatic duct is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I keep getting infections? Could they remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted interventional radiology and advanced endoscopy. Unfortunately, because of where it’s located and your anatomy, they don’t think it can be safely removed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just going to keep causing problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be acting as a nidus for infection, yes. That’s why we’re starting you on IV antibiotics—meropenem—because it worked well for you last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust that. But I was supposed to start doxycycline soon for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But since you flared right after stopping cipro, we think you need a stronger course. We’ll transition you to ertapenem later, which you can take at home through a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A PICC line? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a long-term IV that goes into a vein in your arm. It’s very common for patients like you needing extended antibiotics. We’ll place it before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my other meds—can I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your levothyroxine, omeprazole, and escitalopram. We’ve held your lisinopril and furosemide for now to make sure we don’t mask any signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My cough—is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned it’s dry and been going on for weeks. No fever or chest pain. Likely post-viral. We’ll monitor, but it doesn’t look like pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white count is low but stable, and your liver enzymes are elevated—AST and ALT are up a bit, and alkaline phosphatase is high, which fits with cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet, but it’s early. Your blood cultures came back negative, which is good—no bacteria grew. That’s common with your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we don’t know what’s causing the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. But given your history and symptoms, we’re confident it’s cholangitis. We’re treating it empirically, and you’re already feeling better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is less, and I don’t feel as shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs this morning show your bilirubin has dropped from 1.2 to 0.6, and your alkaline phosphatase is still up but stable. That’s improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll place the PICC line in the morning, and you’ll finish a 14-day course of ertapenem at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then what? Just wait for the next flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend an outpatient MRCP—a special MRI of your bile ducts—to get a better look at that stone. Maybe in the future, we can find a way to address it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. And my colonoscopy follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had pre-cancerous polyps removed before. You’re due for another in a few years, or sooner if your bowel habits change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the chest X-ray after your PICC placement shows it’s in the right spot, in the lower superior vena cava. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How do I care for it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will visit you at home to give the daily IV antibiotic and teach you how to flush the line with saline and heparin to keep it working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—everything restarts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting your lisinopril and furosemide today. All your other medications continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you to go home. Your last dose of IV antibiotic will be in 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule your MRCP and follow up with your liver clinic. Call us if you develop fever, pain, or any redness at the PICC site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you soon in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis complicated by cirrhosis was admitted with recurrent cholangitis, presenting with fever and right upper quadrant pain. She had recently completed a course of ciprofloxacin but developed symptoms consistent with a flare. Imaging confirmed a persistent 7mm stone in the right intrahepatic duct, which could not be removed due to anatomical constraints. She was treated with intravenous meropenem, transitioned to ertapenem via a newly placed PICC line for a 14-day course, and showed clinical and laboratory improvement. Chronic medications were managed, with lisinopril and furosemide held initially and restarted at discharge. She was discharged home with home health support for IV antibiotics and plans for outpatient MRCP and gastroenterology follow-up.
